idiom_name: capability value of primitives handed to a one-method behaviour interface (ResponseWriter / Handler shape)
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, no protected visibility and no virtual dispatch, and embedding is not a substitute: Effective Go states that methods of an embedded type keep the inner type as their receiver, so a promoted primitive can never call the outer type's behaviour. The classic structure is therefore replaced by a capability: the primitives become methods on a small value or interface that is handed to the behaviour, and the behaviour is any type implementing one method - net/http is the canonical instance, where a handler's ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) may compose only the ResponseWriter operations (Header, Write, WriteHeader) plus the optional Flusher/Hijacker interfaces, with the connection internals out of reach. Where the primitives need engine state rather than per-request data, pass a *World or *Sandbox struct instead of an interface; where several behaviours share nothing, keep the sandbox value small and explicit rather than exporting it. The classic base-class shape is only justified when a foreign caller dictates a method set; Go's own answer is accept interfaces and hand capabilities to behaviour.
pitfalls: There is no protected: a primitive is exported to the whole program or lives in the same package, so use an internal/ package or keep the primitive set as unexported methods with exported behaviour - otherwise the sandbox is public API.
Do not emulate the base class with an embedded struct: a promoted primitive has the inner receiver (Effective Go) and cannot reach the outer type's method, so the 'override' silently never runs.
A nil interface holding a typed nil pointer panics on call, so a *Sandbox that may be absent must be checked explicitly rather than passed as an interface value.

Primitives on a shared *Sandbox are often called from several goroutines; either make the sandbox single-goroutine by construction or document and enforce the synchronisation, because the base class here is a value and carries no locking of its own.
